questions.question: Code generation scenario. Your review agent's prompt ends with: 'Only report issues you are highly confident about.' Developers now ignore the agent. A sample of 200 findings shows 41% are naming or formatting remarks that match the file's existing style, and real logic bugs are buried among them. Which change most directly raises precision?

options.A: Replace the confidence line with explicit categories: report logic bugs and security flaws; skip naming, formatting and patterns that match the file's local style.
options.B: Strengthen the existing line to 'Be conservative: only report findings you are at least 90% sure are real problems', so the model holds itself to a higher bar before it writes any finding.
options.C: Keep the prompt as it is, ask the model to attach a confidence score to each finding, and have code drop every finding scored below 0.8 before it is posted to the pull request.
options.D: Move the review to a larger model with extended thinking turned on, so it has more reasoning budget to judge which findings are worth a developer's time.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.1: explicit criteria beat vague instructions. Writing which issue types to report (bugs, security) and which to skip (minor style, local patterns) is the named skill, 'rather than relying on confidence-based filtering'. Lines like 'be conservative' or 'only report high-confidence findings' are named as not improving precision.

why_not.B: A stricter 'be conservative' line is still a vague instruction, and task 4.1 says such lines fail to improve precision.
why_not.C: Confidence-based filtering is the approach 4.1 says to replace with categorical report/skip criteria.
why_not.D: A bigger model does not know which categories your team wants; the missing piece is the criteria, not reasoning power.

questions.objective: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.1 (Tier 1).

questions.question:
Code generation scenario. Your review bot's weekly report reads:

category          posted  dismissed
security              22          2
null-handling         35          6
comment-accuracy     140        126

The comment-accuracy rule in the prompt is: 'Check that comments are accurate.' Developers now say they skip the whole bot, including security findings. What is the best first move?

options.A: Keep all three categories on, and add 'only report comment problems you are very confident about' to the comment-accuracy rule so fewer of those findings are posted next week.
options.B: Turn the bot off for the whole team until every category has been re-tuned and tested, so developers stop seeing any noisy output at all in the meantime.
options.C: Add a severity field to every finding and ask developers to sort by severity, so the important security findings rise to the top of the list in each pull request.
options.D: Switch off only the comment-accuracy category for now, and rewrite its rule to flag a comment only when its claim contradicts what the code does.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.1: high false-positive categories undermine trust in accurate categories. The named skills are temporarily disabling high false-positive categories while improving their prompts, and replacing vague rules ('check that comments are accurate') with explicit ones ('flag comments only when claimed behaviour contradicts actual code behaviour').

why_not.A: A 'very confident' line is a vague instruction that 4.1 says does not fix precision, and it leaves the trust damage in place this week.
why_not.B: Turning off the categories that work (security at 2 of 22 dismissed) throws away good signal; 4.1 says disable only the high false-positive category.
why_not.C: Sorting does not remove the 126 noisy findings, and high false-positive categories still undermine trust in the accurate ones.

questions.objective: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.1 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Multi-agent research scenario. A document-analysis agent extracts each paper's cited sources into a required 'sources' array. Papers with inline citations work well. Papers that list sources only in a bibliography at the end come back with an empty array, even though the instructions describe both layouts in detail. What should you add first?

options.A: Make the 'sources' array require at least one item, so the model cannot return it empty and has to look harder through the paper before it answers.
options.B: Move the extraction to a larger model with a longer context window, so the bibliography at the end of a long paper stays within the model's attention.
options.C: Add two to four examples that show a correct extraction from a bibliography-style paper and from an inline-citation paper, with the expected output for each.
options.D: Expand the instructions with a full paragraph for every citation style you know of (APA, MLA, numbered, footnotes), so the model has a written rule for each layout.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.2: few-shot examples show correct handling of varied document structures (inline citations vs bibliographies) and address empty or null extraction of required fields. They are the most effective technique when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent output. Use 2 to 4 targeted examples.

why_not.A: Forcing a non-empty array pushes the model to invent sources when it is unsure, which is a fabrication risk, not a fix.
why_not.B: The paper already fits in context; the model is missing a demonstration of the layout, not more window.
why_not.D: The instructions already describe both layouts; 4.2 says examples work when detailed instructions alone give inconsistent results.

questions.objective: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.2 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Choose two. Code generation scenario. Your review agent's findings vary in shape: some have a file and line, some have no suggested fix, and severity words change from run to run. It also flags a defensive early-return pattern your team likes. Which two additions best fix both problems while still letting the agent judge new code it has not seen?

options.A: A line in capital letters telling the agent to 'USE THE SAME FORMAT EVERY TIME AND DO NOT FLAG GOOD CODE', placed at the top and the bottom of the prompt.
options.B: Two or three example findings written in the exact shape you want: location, issue, severity and suggested fix.
options.C: A list of 40 example findings covering every pattern the team has ever discussed, so the agent can match each new finding to the closest one on the list.
options.D: An example that shows the early-return pattern, says it is acceptable, and explains why it is not flagged, next to an example of a genuine issue that looks similar.
options.E: Setting temperature to 0 so the output format and the judgement are the same on every run.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.2: few-shot examples that show the desired output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) give consistency, and examples that separate acceptable code patterns from genuine issues reduce false positives while still letting the model generalise to new patterns.

why_not.A: Shouting the rule is still an instruction alone, and 4.2 says instructions alone are what produced the inconsistency.
why_not.C: A huge catalogue pushes the agent toward matching listed cases; 4.2 wants a few targeted examples that let it generalise.
why_not.E: Lower temperature can make one run repeatable, but it does not teach the format or the acceptable-pattern judgement.

questions.objective: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.2 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. Your system prompt says 'Respond with JSON only, no other text.' About 3% of replies still break the downstream parser: some start with 'Here is the JSON:', some have an unescaped quote inside a vendor name. Which change removes this class of failure?

options.A: Define an extraction tool whose input_schema is the JSON you need, and read the data from the tool_use block's input, not from the reply text.
options.B: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening '{' so the model starts inside the JSON object and cannot add any introductory sentence before the data.
options.C: Add a complete example JSON object to the system prompt and repeat 'JSON only, no prose, escape all quotes' at the end of the user message as well.
options.D: Wrap the parser in a try block and, when parsing fails, send the same request again until a reply parses, with a limit of three attempts per document.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.3: tool use with JSON schemas is 'the most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output, eliminating JSON syntax errors'. The skill is defining extraction tools with JSON schemas as input parameters and reading the data from the tool_use response. What changed since: current docs also offer strict tool use (strict: true) and JSON outputs (output_config.format) [platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs].

why_not.B: Prefill is less reliable than tool use and does nothing about escaping. What changed since: Claude 4.6 and later models return a 400 invalid_request_error for a prefilled last assistant message [platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors].
why_not.C: Prompt-only JSON is still prompt-only; stronger wording makes errors rarer, not impossible.
why_not.D: Blind retries treat the symptom and pay for extra calls; the failure class stays.

questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1); platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs; platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors.

questions.question:
Structured data extraction scenario. Your request sends one tool, extract_invoice, with "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"}. For a short invoice the response is:

{"stop_reason": "end_turn",
 "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This invoice is from Acme Ltd for $1,240, due 3 March."}]}

Your code expected a tool_use block and crashed. What is the smallest change that guarantees the tool is called on every invoice?

options.A: Check the reply text for the words 'invoice' and 'due', and when they appear, parse the amount and date out of the sentence with a regular expression.
options.B: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to write the full tool call after its short summary, and loop until stop_reason comes back as tool_use.
options.C: Add 'You must call extract_invoice for every invoice; do not answer in plain text' to the system prompt, and keep tool_choice set to auto so the model can still decline bad inputs.
options.D: Change tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} so the model has to call that named tool on this request.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.3: tool_choice 'auto' means the model may return text instead of calling a tool; forced selection ({"type": "tool", "name": ...}) means it must call that named tool. With a single extraction tool, forcing it is the exam's answer. What changed since: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any and tool return a 400 whatever the thinking setting, and with manual extended thinking they error on any model. Current docs say to use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.A: Parsing prose is the fragile path that structured output exists to remove.
why_not.B: The reply was not cut off (stop_reason is end_turn, not max_tokens), so more tokens change nothing.
why_not.C: With auto the model may still return text; a prompt line only makes that rarer.

questions.objective: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Choose two. Structured data extraction scenario. The team has moved invoice extraction to tool use with a strict JSON schema. A teammate now proposes deleting the code-side validation layer. Which two statements should guide the decision?

options.A: Tool use with a JSON schema removes JSON syntax errors, so the parser no longer needs to handle malformed JSON.
options.B: The schema can still be met while a value lands in the wrong field, such as ship-to in bill-to.
options.C: Prefilling the reply with '{' gives the same guarantee as tool use, so either method lets you drop validation.
options.D: Because the schema lists line_items and total, the model's line items are now guaranteed to add up to the total.
options.E: Once a schema is enforced, review routing can be removed, because a schema-valid extraction is a correct extraction.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.3: strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors (line items that don't sum to total, values in wrong fields). Keep the semantic validation in code.

why_not.C: Prefill gives no schema guarantee, so it is weaker than tool use and still needs validation.
why_not.D: Sums are a semantic rule; 4.3 says schemas do not prevent line items that don't sum to the total.
why_not.E: Schema-valid is not the same as correct; semantic errors still need checks and review.

questions.objective: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1).

options.A: Add a cleanup step after extraction that deletes any po_number containing '0000' or 'N/A', so made-up values never reach the finance system.
options.B: Let po_number be null ("type": ["string", "null"], or make it optional) and tell the model to return null when the document has no purchase order.
options.C: When validation finds a PO value that is not in the purchase-order system, send the document back with that error message and ask the model to try again.
options.D: Keep the schema as it is and add 'Do not invent a purchase order number' to the prompt, so the model leaves the value blank in its own words.

Confirmed: type arrays such as "type": ["string", "null"] are allowed in strict schemas (listed under union types, with a higher compile cost) [platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs].

why_not.C: The value is absent from the source, and 4.4 says retries do not help when the information simply isn't there.
why_not.D: The schema still demands a string, so the model is still pushed to fill it; the prompt line fights the schema.

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. Your schema has "doc_type": {"enum": ["invoice", "receipt", "credit_note"]}. Suppliers have started sending pro-forma invoices and delivery notes, and the model files them all as "invoice". Some scans are so faint that even a person can't tell the type. Which schema change handles both problems?

options.A: Remove the enum and make doc_type a free-text string, so the model can write whatever type it sees and nothing is ever forced into the wrong value.
options.B: Keep the three values and add a doc_type_confidence number, so low-confidence 'invoice' answers can be spotted later in reporting.
options.C: Add "other" with a separate doc_type_detail string for new categories, and add "unclear" for documents whose type can't be told from the page.
options.D: Add 'proforma' and 'delivery_note' to the enum now, and add each new type to the enum by hand whenever finance reports another one they spotted in the queue.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.3: add enum values like "unclear" for ambiguous cases and "other" + a detail field for extensible categorisation.

why_not.A: Free text loses consistent categories, so downstream code can't group or route by type.
why_not.B: A confidence number still forces a wrong label and adds no place to say what the type really is.
why_not.D: Chasing every new type by hand means each new type is misfiled until someone notices; it does not handle the faint scans at all.

questions.objective: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Choose two. Structured data extraction scenario. Receipts show currency as '$', 'USD', 'US dollars' or nothing at all, and dates as '03/04/26', '4 March 2026' or '2026-03-04'. Downstream code needs one format for each. Which two changes fit best?

options.A: Use an enum of currency codes plus "other" with a detail string, and allow null when the receipt shows no currency.
options.B: Make currency a required, non-null field so every receipt carries a currency value, even when it shows none.
options.C: Put format rules in the prompt (dates as YYYY-MM-DD, currency as a code) alongside the strict output schema.
options.D: Leave both fields as free text and write regular expressions after extraction to clean each variant you find.
options.E: Add one few-shot example of a US receipt in perfect ISO format, so the model copies that format for every receipt.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.3: include format normalisation rules in prompts alongside strict output schemas to handle inconsistent source formatting; use enums with "other" + detail, and nullable fields when the source may lack the value.

why_not.B: Required and non-null with no source value pushes the model to fabricate a currency.
why_not.D: Pushing all cleanup into regex after the fact gives up the schema's help and breaks on each new variant.
why_not.E: One example of only one format does not show how to handle the varied inputs.

questions.objective: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. An intake pipeline receives contracts, invoices and shipping manifests in one queue, with no label saying which is which. You have three extraction tools, one per document type. On some documents the model writes a short summary instead of calling any tool. What tool_choice setting fits?

options.A: "tool_choice": {"type": "any"}, so the model must call one of the three extraction tools but still picks the one that fits.
options.B: "tool_choice": {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}, because invoices are the most common type, and let the invoice schema absorb the other documents.
options.C: "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"} with a system prompt line saying 'Call exactly one extraction tool per document; do not reply with a summary'.
options.D: Merge the three schemas into one large extract_document tool with every field optional, then force that single tool on every request.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.3: set tool_choice "any" to guarantee structured output when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown. "any" means the model must call a tool but can choose which. What changed since: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any and tool return a 400 whatever the thinking setting, and with manual extended thinking they error on any model. Current docs say to use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.B: Forcing the invoice tool makes contracts and manifests go through the wrong schema.
why_not.C: auto still lets the model answer in text; the prompt line only makes it rarer.
why_not.D: One giant all-optional schema loses the per-type structure and invites empty or misplaced fields.

questions.question:
Structured data extraction scenario. The first request of each document's run is:

"tools": [extract_metadata, lookup_vendor, geocode_address],
"tool_choice": {"type": "any"}

The design says extract_metadata must run before any enrichment. Logs show the first call is lookup_vendor in about 1 run in 10, using a vendor name the model guessed from the file name. What is the right fix?

options.A: Force extract_metadata with "tool_choice": {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first request, then let the model choose in follow-up turns.
options.B: Keep "any", and since extract_metadata is already first in the tools array, add a sentence to its description saying it must be called before the other two tools.
options.C: Remove lookup_vendor and geocode_address from the agent entirely, so extract_metadata is the only tool it can ever call during the run.
options.D: Keep "any" and add a system prompt rule: 'Step 1 is always extract_metadata. Do not call enrichment tools until metadata exists.'

questions.rationale: Task statements 4.3 and 2.3: force a specific tool with tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} to ensure it runs before enrichment steps, then process subsequent steps in follow-up turns. "any" lets the model pick which tool, and tool order in the array is not a control. What changed since: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any and tool return a 400 whatever the thinking setting, and with manual extended thinking they error on any model. Current docs say to use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.B: The order of the tools array does not force which tool runs first, and a description line is still guidance, not a guarantee.
why_not.C: Removing the enrichment tools breaks the later steps the workflow needs.
why_not.D: A prompt rule lowers the miss rate but does not make it zero.

options.B: The same original prompt and document, sent again unchanged, since a second independent attempt will often land on the correct reading by itself.
options.C: No retry: overwrite stated_total with the calculated 1240.00 so the record is internally consistent, and post it to the ledger.

A format or misread error is the kind a retry can fix.

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. For a set of service contracts, contract_end_date keeps failing validation after two retries with error feedback. The contracts say only: 'Term ends as set out in Schedule B of the Master Agreement.' Schedule B is a separate file that is not sent to the model. What should the pipeline do?

options.A: Raise the retry limit from two to five and add the phrase 'look carefully for the end date' to the error feedback, since the date is clearly important to the business.
options.B: Switch these contracts to a larger model with extended thinking, which is better at working out dates from indirect wording like 'as set out in'.
options.C: Add few-shot examples of contracts where the end date was found in the body text, so the model learns where end dates usually appear.
options.D: Stop retrying, since the date isn't in the input: return null with a note that Schedule B defines it, then send Schedule B or route to a reviewer.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.4: retries are ineffective when the required information is absent from the source (for example, it exists only in an external document not provided), versus format or structural errors, where they succeed.

why_not.A: More retries can't find information that isn't in the input; 4.4 names this as the limit of retry.
why_not.B: No model can read a date from a file it was never sent.
why_not.C: Examples help with format and layout, not with data that lives in another document.

questions.question: Choose two. Structured data extraction scenario. Some supplier invoices are themselves wrong: the printed total doesn't match the lines, or the header date and the footer date differ. Finance wants these caught, not silently fixed. Which two schema additions support that?

options.A: A single boolean 'is_valid' that the model sets to false whenever anything on the invoice looks off to it.
options.B: A calculated_total field alongside stated_total, so code can compare the two and flag a gap.
options.C: A conflict_detected boolean (with a short note) for when the document contradicts itself, such as two different dates.
options.D: Dropping stated_total from the schema, since code can always compute the total from the lines.
options.E: An instruction to adjust the line items so they add up to the printed total before the tool is called.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.4: design self-correction validation flows by extracting "calculated_total" alongside "stated_total" to flag discrepancies, and adding "conflict_detected" booleans for inconsistent source data.

why_not.A: One vague flag says nothing about what is wrong, so code can't check or route it precisely.
why_not.D: Without the stated total you can no longer detect a supplier's arithmetic error.
why_not.E: Adjusting lines to match is exactly the silent fixing finance does not want.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. Developers dismiss about a third of your review agent's findings, but nobody can say which kinds of code trigger the dismissed ones. You want data to improve the prompt systematically. What should you add?

options.A: An automatic rule that turns off any category once its dismissal rate passes 30% for two weeks in a row, with no further review.
options.B: A detected_pattern field on each structured finding naming the code construct that triggered it, so dismissals can be grouped and analysed by pattern.
options.C: A lower confidence threshold for posting, so more findings appear and the dismissal rate is spread across a larger number of findings.
options.D: A free-text comment box shown when a developer dismisses a finding, collected into a weekly document for the team lead to read through.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.4: feedback loop design tracks which code constructs trigger findings (a detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns.

why_not.A: Auto-disabling hides the problem without learning which pattern causes it.
why_not.C: Posting more findings lowers the rate on paper and adds noise; it gives no insight.
why_not.D: Free text is hard to analyse at scale and does not tie dismissals to code constructs.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. Your review agent posts about 400 findings a month, and developers dismiss about 45% of them. Each structured finding has file, line, severity and message. Before you change the prompt, you want to learn which kinds of code construct cause the dismissals. What should you add?

options.A: A detected_pattern field on each finding naming the construct that triggered it, so dismissals can be grouped.
options.B: A free-text reasoning paragraph on each finding, so a reviewer can read the dismissed ones and look for themes.
options.C: A confidence score on each finding, so you can see whether the low-confidence findings are the ones being dismissed.
options.D: A higher severity bar for posting, so fewer findings are posted next month and the dismissal rate falls by itself.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.4: feedback loop design means tracking which code constructs trigger findings (a detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns; the named skill is adding detected_pattern fields to structured findings to enable analysis of false positive patterns when developers dismiss findings. Once dismissals are grouped by pattern, you fix the worst pattern's criteria (4.1).

why_not.B: Free text can't be grouped or counted by code; a structured field can.
why_not.C: Confidence says how sure the model is, not which construct triggered the finding, so it can't point you to the criteria to fix.
why_not.D: Posting fewer findings hides the false positives without showing which pattern causes them.

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. Claims arrive all day. Each one must be extracted and loaded within 32 hours of arriving. Loading the batch results takes 2 hours. You use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours. What is the longest gap you can allow between batch submissions and still always meet the deadline?

options.A: 6 hours: a claim arriving just after a submission waits up to 6 h, then up to 24 h of processing, then 2 h of loading, which is 32 h.
options.B: 8 hours, because 32 minus 24 leaves 8 hours, and loading can overlap with the next batch's processing, so the 2 hours don't count against the deadline.
options.C: 24 hours (one batch a day), because most batches finish within an hour, so the real total is far below 32 hours on almost every day.
options.D: Any gap works if you also keep a synchronous fallback that retries claims older than 30 hours, so the batch interval is not the thing that sets the deadline.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.5: calculate batch submission frequency from SLA constraints, given the up-to-24-hour processing window and no guaranteed latency SLA. Worst case = submission gap + 24 h + downstream time. 32 - 24 - 2 = 6 hours. (Original numbers, not the guide's example.)

why_not.B: The worst-case claim still needs its own 2 hours of loading after its results arrive: 8 + 24 + 2 = 34 hours.
why_not.C: Planning on the typical 1 hour ignores the up-to-24-hour window with no latency SLA.
why_not.D: A fallback is a patch for a bad interval, not a design that meets the SLA; it also spends full price.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. An agent writes a database migration, then in the same session you ask it to 'critically review the migration you just wrote'. It approves the migration, which later drops an index that production queries need. Which design most improves the review?

options.A: Ask the same session to review the migration twice in a row, and only approve the change when both passes agree that there are no problems.
options.B: Keep the review in the same session but turn on extended thinking for the review step, so the model reasons harder about its own decisions before it approves anything.
options.C: Give the same session a detailed review checklist (indexes, locks, rollback steps) and require it to tick each item before it can approve the migration.
options.D: Send the migration to a second, independent Claude instance that has none of the generating session's reasoning, with its own review instructions.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.6: a model keeps reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its own decisions in the same session; independent review instances without that context catch subtle issues better than self-review instructions or extended thinking.

why_not.A: Two passes in the same context share the same blind spots.
why_not.B: 4.6 says independent instances beat extended thinking, because the same session keeps its own reasoning context.
why_not.C: A checklist helps, but the reviewer still carries the generator's reasoning and is less likely to question it.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. Your review pipeline posts every finding straight to the pull request. Senior reviewers have about an hour a day and want to spend it on findings that might be wrong, not on obvious ones. Which addition fits?

options.A: A random 10% of all findings sent to the senior reviewers each day, so their time is spread fairly across every category and every repository.
options.B: A single confidence score for each whole pull request, so pull requests below the threshold get a senior reviewer and everything else is posted directly.
options.C: A verification pass where the model reports confidence for each finding, with thresholds calibrated on labelled examples to route the doubtful ones.
options.D: Posting only findings the model labels "severity": "high" and dropping the rest, so the senior reviewers see far fewer findings each day.

questions.rationale: Task statement 4.6: run verification passes where the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding to enable calibrated review routing. Task 5.5 adds calibrating thresholds on labelled validation sets.

why_not.A: Random sampling spends scarce time on findings that are clearly right.
why_not.B: One score per pull request hides which individual finding is uncertain.
why_not.D: Severity is not confidence; dropping lower-severity findings loses real issues and still posts wrong high-severity ones.

questions.question:
Multi-agent research scenario. The analysis subagent's last step writes a plain-text summary for the coordinator. Its final request is:

{"tools": [search_papers, get_citation_metadata, fetch_table],
 "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"},
 "messages": [... 14 turns, including earlier tool_use and tool_result blocks ...,
   {"role": "user", "content": "Now write the final summary."}]}

About 1 run in 5, the reply is another search_papers call instead of the summary, and the step overruns. What is the best change to this final request?

options.A: Set "tool_choice": {"type": "any"} on the final request, so the model has to commit to a single decisive action and stops looping between searches.
options.B: Set "tool_choice": {"type": "none"} on the final request, so the model keeps the tool definitions and history but replies in text only.
options.C: Keep "auto" and end the user message with 'Do not call any more tools. Write the summary now.', so the model knows the search phase is over.
options.D: Delete the tools array and every tool_use and tool_result block from the history, so the model has nothing left to call when it writes.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3 (configure tool choice). "auto" lets the model decide, so it may call a tool or reply in text; "any" makes it call some tool; a named tool forces that tool. The current docs also list "none", which stops the model using any tools [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. "none" is in the docs, not in the exam guide's list, so on the exam expect the three guide options; the idea to keep is: pick the tool_choice that matches what this turn must produce. If an exam item offers only the guide's three options, remember that "auto" can reply in text, while "any" and forced selection cannot.

why_not.A: "any" forces a tool call, which is the opposite of what the final step needs.
why_not.C: With "auto" the model may still call a tool; a prompt line only makes that rarer.
why_not.D: Stripping the history throws away the findings the summary is built from.

questions.objective: Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1); platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. A review step looks at one changed file per request. It has two tools: record_findings (a list of issues) and record_clean (the file needs no comments). Your pipeline needs exactly one of these calls for every file. With tool_choice auto, some files come back as a chat reply like 'Looks fine to me!', and the pipeline loses track of them. What should you set?

options.A: "tool_choice": {"type": "any"}, so the model must call a tool on every file but can still choose record_clean when nothing is wrong.
options.B: "tool_choice": {"type": "none"}, and parse the reply text for the words 'fine' or 'issue' to decide which record to write.
options.C: "tool_choice": {"type": "tool", "name": "record_findings"}, so every file gets a findings call, with an empty list when clean.
options.D: Keep "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"} and add 'Always finish by calling record_findings or record_clean' to the system prompt.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3: set tool_choice "any" to guarantee the model calls a tool rather than returning conversational text. "any" means some tool must be called, but it does not decide which one, so the model can still pick record_clean. Forcing a named tool fixes which tool runs, which is wrong when the right tool depends on the input. What changed since: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any and tool return a 400 whatever the thinking setting, and with manual extended thinking they error on any model. Current docs say to use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.B: "none" blocks the tools and puts you back to parsing prose.
why_not.C: Forcing record_findings removes the model's choice, pushing it to report issues on clean files.
why_not.D: "auto" still lets a chat reply slip through; the prompt line only makes it rarer.

questions.question:
Structured data extraction scenario. Your agent loop builds every request the same way:

while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model=M, tools=TOOLS, messages=history,
        tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"})
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    history += run_tools(resp)

The run never reaches the enrichment tools and only stops when it hits your cost limit. What is the smallest correct fix?

options.A: Force extract_metadata only on the first request, and send later requests with tool_choice auto (or any) so the model can call enrichment tools and finish.
options.B: Change the break test to stop when stop_reason is "end_turn" or "max_tokens", so the loop can finish once the model has nothing more to add.
options.C: Move extract_metadata to the end of TOOLS, so the model sees the enrichment tools first and moves on to them after the first turn of the run.
options.D: Add an iteration cap of 10 to the loop and treat reaching the cap as the normal signal that the extraction is finished.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3: use forced selection to ensure a specific tool is called first, then process subsequent steps in follow-up turns. Forcing the same tool on every turn means the model must call it again each time (tool_choice tool = must call that named tool), so the loop never ends. What changed since: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any and tool return a 400 whatever the thinking setting, and with manual extended thinking they error on any model. Current docs say to use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.B: While the tool is forced, every reply is a tool_use for extract_metadata, so the loop never sees end_turn.
why_not.C: Tool order doesn't override a forced tool_choice.
why_not.D: A cap as the completion signal is an anti-pattern; it hides the bug and cuts off real work.

questions.question: Choose two. Multi-agent research scenario. The analysis subagent has three tools: load_dataset_manifest, query_dataset and plot_series. Each run must call load_dataset_manifest first. After that, the model should pick whatever tools it needs and finish with a written answer. Which two settings give that behaviour?

options.A: After the manifest result comes back, send every later request with "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"} so the model can choose.
options.B: Use "tool_choice": {"type": "any"} on every request, so the model keeps calling tools until the analysis is done.
options.C: List load_dataset_manifest first in the tools array, since the model works through tools in the order they are listed.
options.D: On the first request, force the manifest tool: "tool_choice": {"type": "tool", "name": "load_dataset_manifest"}.
options.E: Send the forced load_dataset_manifest choice on every request in the run, so the order cannot slip on later turns.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3: use tool_choice forced selection to ensure a specific tool is called first, then process subsequent steps in follow-up turns. "auto" on the follow-up turns lets the model choose tools or answer in text. Tool order in the array is not a control. What changed since: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any and tool return a 400 whatever the thinking setting, and with manual extended thinking they error on any model. Current docs say to use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.B: "any" on every turn forbids the final text answer, and it still does not make the manifest come first.
why_not.C: The order of the tools array does not control which tool is called first.
why_not.E: Forcing the same tool every turn means the model must call it again and again and never reaches the other tools.

questions.question:
Structured data extraction scenario. Before cutting human review, you pull last quarter's audited results:

segment                      docs    accuracy
all documents              48,200      97.1%
typed invoices             39,500      98.9%
handwritten receipts        6,100      86.4%
faxed invoices: total_amount 2,600      74.0%

Leadership wants to stop reviewing every document 'because we are at 97%'. What should you recommend?

options.A: Reduce review only for the proven segment (typed invoices), keep it for handwritten receipts and faxed totals, and check each segment first.
options.B: Agree, and cut review for all documents now, since 97.1% is above the 95% target, then add a monthly random audit of 1% of all documents to watch the trend.
options.C: Keep full review for everything until overall accuracy passes 99%, since the overall number is the one leadership reports on and must reach the bar first.
options.D: Cut review only for documents whose model confidence is above 0.9, since high-confidence extractions are reliable whatever their document type.

questions.rationale: Task statement 5.5: aggregate accuracy (for example 97% overall) may mask poor performance on specific document types or fields; validate accuracy by document type and field segment before automating high-confidence extractions.

why_not.B: The 97% overall figure hides a 74% field on faxes; cutting review there ships many errors.
why_not.C: Waiting on the overall number keeps reviewers on 39,500 typed invoices that are already accurate.
why_not.D: Confidence is not proven reliable for each segment until it has been calibrated and checked by segment.

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. You want to send only some extractions to reviewers. The model already returns a confidence value for each field. In a spot check, fields marked 0.95 were wrong about as often as fields marked 0.80. How should you set the review thresholds?

options.A: Ask the model in the prompt to 'be honest and well calibrated when reporting confidence', then keep using the raw scores as the thresholds.
options.B: Use 0.9 for every field, because a 90% cutoff is the industry norm for automated extraction and keeps the review rules simple for everyone.
options.C: Replace field scores with a single document-level confidence, since one number per document is easier to calibrate than many per-field numbers.
options.D: Calibrate the field-level scores against a labelled validation set, then set each field's threshold from how often fields at each score turn out correct.

questions.rationale: Task statement 5.5: have models output field-level confidence scores, then calibrate review thresholds using labelled validation sets.

why_not.A: Asking for honesty does not calibrate anything; you still need labelled data.
why_not.B: The spot check shows the raw scores don't mean what they say; a fixed cutoff on uncalibrated scores routes the wrong items.
why_not.C: A document-level score hides which field needs review.

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. High-confidence extractions now skip review. Three months later, a supplier changes its invoice layout and tax amounts start landing in the discount field, all with high confidence. Nobody notices for weeks. What would have caught this early?

options.A: Stratified random sampling of the high-confidence extractions (by supplier, document type and field) for ongoing error-rate checks.
options.B: Sending every extraction with confidence under 0.95 to reviewers, so more of the borderline output gets a human look before it is posted.
options.C: Turning review back on for everything for a week every quarter, then switching it off again once the accuracy numbers look stable.
options.D: A rule that re-runs the extraction whenever a field is empty, so any document where the model missed a value gets a second chance automatically.

questions.rationale: Task statement 5.5: stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions measures ongoing error rates and detects novel error patterns.

why_not.B: The bad fields were high confidence, so a lower-confidence filter never sees them.
why_not.C: Periodic full review costs a lot and still leaves up to three months of undetected errors.
why_not.D: The fields weren't empty; they had values in the wrong place.

questions.question: Choose two. Structured data extraction scenario. Reviewers can handle about 300 documents a day out of 4,000. Schema validation already rejects malformed output before this step. Which two kinds of extraction should take those review slots first?

options.A: Extractions where the source document is ambiguous or contradicts itself, for example conflict_detected is true.
options.B: A random 300 documents from the day's whole intake, so reviewers see an unbiased mix of every kind of document.
options.C: Extractions where the model's output text was longest, since long outputs give the model more room to make mistakes.
options.D: Extractions that failed schema validation, so reviewers can fix the JSON by hand before it is loaded.
options.E: Extractions where a field's calibrated confidence is below its threshold.

questions.rationale: Task statement 5.5: route extractions with low model confidence or ambiguous or contradictory source documents to human review, prioritising limited reviewer capacity.

why_not.B: Pure random sampling across everything doesn't spend scarce reviewer time where errors are likely.
why_not.C: Output length isn't a calibrated signal of error.
why_not.D: Schema failures are already caught and retried in code; they are not a good use of reviewers.

questions.question:
Developer productivity scenario. A new hire says Claude keeps using npm in your repo, while for the tech lead it always uses pnpm. On the tech lead's laptop:

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md:
  - Use pnpm, never npm.
  - Run `pnpm test:unit` before any commit.

repo/CLAUDE.md:
  - Service overview and folder map.

What is the right fix?

options.A: Move the pnpm and test rules into the project's CLAUDE.md (repo/CLAUDE.md or repo/.claude/CLAUDE.md) and commit it, so everyone who clones the repo gets them.
options.B: Ask the new hire to copy the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md onto their own laptop, so both machines carry the same personal instructions from now on.
options.C: Put the two rules in a CLAUDE.local.md file at the repo root, since that file sits next to the project CLAUDE.md and is loaded alongside it for everyone.
options.D: Ask the new hire to start each session with 'use pnpm and run unit tests before committing', so the rule is always in the prompt when it matters.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.1: user-level instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply only to that user and are not shared through version control. Diagnosing a new team member not receiving instructions because they are user-level, not project-level, is a named skill. Project-level is .claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md.

why_not.B: Copying personal files by hand drifts again the next time either person edits theirs; team rules belong in version control.
why_not.C: CLAUDE.local.md is for personal project preferences and is meant to be gitignored, so teammates don't get it [code.claude.com/docs/en/memory].
why_not.D: Typing the rule each time is easy to forget and isn't shared.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. A monorepo has packages/payments, packages/web and packages/data. Standards live in docs/standards/: api.md, pci.md, react.md, sql.md. Payments needs api and pci; web needs react; data needs sql and api. Package maintainers know which standards apply. How should you include them?

options.A: In each package's CLAUDE.md, add @ imports for only the standards that package needs, for example @../../docs/standards/pci.md in payments.
options.B: Ask developers to type 'follow docs/standards/pci.md' in their prompt whenever they start work in the payments package.
options.C: Paste all four standards files into the root CLAUDE.md, so every package sees every standard and nothing can be missed by mistake.
options.D: Put the four standards in each maintainer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, since maintainers are the ones who know which standards apply to their package.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.1: the @import syntax references external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular, importing the specific standards files relevant to each package based on maintainer knowledge. Relative import paths resolve from the file that contains the import [code.claude.com/docs/en/memory].

why_not.B: Typed reminders depend on memory and aren't shared through the repo.
why_not.C: Every package then loads standards it doesn't need, and a monolithic file is what 3.1 says to avoid.
why_not.D: User-level files aren't shared with teammates.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. Today only, you need Claude to rewrite src/billing/invoice.ts so it follows a 300-line vendor spec in docs/vendor/acme-v3.md. No one else will need the spec after this change ships. Where should the spec reach Claude?

options.A: Add @docs/vendor/acme-v3.md to the project CLAUDE.md, so the spec is loaded at the start of every session until someone remembers to remove it.
options.B: Paste the whole spec into the project CLAUDE.md under a heading, so it is version-controlled and teammates can review it in the pull request.
options.C: Reference it in this session's prompt, for example 'Update @src/billing/invoice.ts to follow @docs/vendor/acme-v3.md', and leave CLAUDE.md unchanged.
options.D: Copy the full spec into a new .claude/rules/acme.md file with no paths field, so it is available as a rule for every task in the project.

questions.rationale: Task statements 3.1 and 3.2: CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded, universal standards; one-off task context goes in the prompt. An @ file reference in the prompt brings in that exact file for this task only (practice, not doc: prompt @-mention behaviour is described in Claude Code docs, not the exam guide).

why_not.B: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded, universal standards, not one-off task material.

questions.question: Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. You are cleaning up what goes where. Which two items belong in the project CLAUDE.md (loaded every session, shared through git), rather than in a one-off prompt or a personal file?

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. A developer says Claude follows the logging rules on Monday's session but ignores them on Tuesday's, in the same repo. You aren't sure which instruction files each session is loading. What is the best first diagnostic step?

options.A: Move the logging rules into a PreToolUse hook, since hooks always run and so the question of which file is loaded no longer matters.
options.B: Copy the logging rules into every CLAUDE.md file in the repository, so whichever file happens to be loaded will contain the rules.
options.C: Reinstall Claude Code on the developer's machine, since inconsistent behaviour between sessions usually points to a corrupted local install.
options.D: Run /memory in the session where the rules are ignored, to see which memory files are actually loaded, and compare with a session where they work.

(One common cause: a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads only when Claude reads or edits files there [code.claude.com/docs/en/memory].) What changed since: in current Claude Code, /memory lists and opens the memory files, and /context lists, under Memory files, the CLAUDE.md files loaded at launch; a subfolder CLAUDE.md loads later, when Claude reads a file there, and a "Loaded …" line with its path appears in the terminal; path-scoped rules also load later, and the InstructionsLoaded hook can log them [code.claude.com/docs/en/memory]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.A: Logging style is guidance, not a must-never-happen rule; and you still haven't diagnosed the problem.
why_not.B: Duplicating rules spreads drift and doesn't explain the cause.
why_not.C: Nothing points to a broken install; check what's loaded first.

questions.question:
Code generation scenario. The file .claude/rules/terraform.md starts with:

---
paths:
  - "infra/**/*.tf"
---
# Terraform rules
- Pin every provider version.

Terraform files live in infra/, but also in modules/network/ and services/*/deploy/. When Claude edits modules/network/main.tf, it ignores the rule. What is the smallest fix?

options.A: Delete the paths block, so the rule is loaded in every session and cannot be missed, whatever file Claude is working on.
options.B: Move the Terraform rules into the root CLAUDE.md, since the root file is always loaded and covers every folder in the repository.
options.C: Change the glob to "**/*.tf", so the rule loads whenever Claude works with any Terraform file, whatever folder it is in.
options.D: Copy terraform.md into a CLAUDE.md file in modules/network/ and in every services/*/deploy/ folder, so each folder carries its own copy of the rule.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.3: .claude/rules/ files use YAML frontmatter paths with glob patterns; use globs to apply conventions by file type regardless of directory. The glob infra/**/*.tf only matches under infra/. Path-scoped rules trigger when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file [code.claude.com/docs/en/memory].

why_not.A: A rule with no paths field loads in every session, adding irrelevant context and tokens.
why_not.B: Same cost problem as deleting the paths block: always loaded even when nobody is touching Terraform.
why_not.D: Directory copies drift apart and miss new folders; 3.3 prefers glob rules for conventions spread across directories.

rules/sql-migrations.md (no frontmatter, 600 lines)
rules/api.md           (no frontmatter, 350 lines)

Most sessions are front-end work, yet token use is high and Claude sometimes applies migration rules to React files. Which change fits?

options.D: Delete sql-migrations.md and api.md, and ask developers to paste those rules into their prompt when they do migration or API work.

why_not.B: Merging keeps everything always loaded; it also undoes the modular split 3.1 recommends.
why_not.C: User-level rules aren't shared through the repo and still load for that user everywhere.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. A bug report includes a stack trace pointing at one line in src/cart/total.ts: a discount can be undefined, and the code multiplies by it. The fix is a guard in that one function plus a unit test. How should you work with Claude Code?

options.B: Start in plan mode, so Claude explores the whole cart module and writes a design before it touches the file, in case the bug has a deeper cause.
options.C: Use direct execution: ask Claude to add the guard in that function and the unit test, then run the tests.
options.D: Send an Explore subagent to map every place discounts are used across the codebase, then decide on an approach once it reports back.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.4: direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes, such as a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace. Plan mode is for large-scale, multi-file or architectural changes.

why_not.A: The interview pattern helps in unfamiliar domains with open design questions; this one is clear.
why_not.B: Plan mode is for large, multi-approach or architectural changes; it adds overhead to a clear one-file fix.
why_not.D: Broad discovery isn't needed when the stack trace names the line.

questions.question: Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. You must move your notification system from polling a database table to an event queue. options.D: Use plan mode to explore the code and compare the two designs, then switch to direct execution to carry out the chosen plan.

why_not.C: One giant prompt skips the investigation and still exhausts context.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. You ask Claude to write a function that turns free-form phone numbers into one format. You describe the rules in a long paragraph. options.B: Rewrite the paragraph to be longer and more precise, listing every rule as a numbered bullet with an explanation of why the rule exists.
options.C: Give two or three concrete input and output pairs that cover the tricky cases, for example '+44 20 7946 0958 ext 12' and the exact string you expect back.
options.D: Ask Claude to try again with extended thinking on, so it reasons more carefully about the description it already has.

why_not.B: The problem is that prose is being read inconsistently; more prose keeps the same weakness.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. You need a rate limiter that handles bursts, clock changes and 10,000 requests a second. Past attempts looked fine in review but broke in production on edge cases. Which way of working with Claude is most likely to converge on a correct version?

options.A: Ask Claude to write the limiter first, then ask it to write tests for the code it wrote, and fix whatever those tests reveal about the code.
options.B: Describe all the edge cases in one long prompt and ask for a finished limiter in one go, so the code is designed with every case in mind from the start.
options.C: Ask Claude to implement the limiter, then review it line by line yourself and send back a list of comments after each review round.
options.D: Write tests first for normal use, edge cases and the throughput target, then have Claude implement and iterate on each test failure.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.5: test-driven iteration means writing test suites covering expected behaviour, edge cases and performance requirements before implementation, then iterating by sharing test failures.

why_not.A: Tests written from the code tend to confirm what the code does, not what it should do.
why_not.B: A single shot gives no feedback loop when edge cases fail.
why_not.C: Manual review missed these edge cases before; failing tests are more precise feedback.

why_not.B: You can't specify considerations you haven't thought of yet; that's what the interview surfaces.

questions.question:
Code generation scenario. After a first pass on a data migration script, your notes say:

1. Rows with NULL email crash the script.
2. The new dedupe step and the batch size together cause the script to skip rows at batch edges.
3. The batch-size change also breaks the progress counter that dedupe relies on.
4. A log message has a typo.

How should you give this feedback to Claude?

options.A: Send issues 2 and 3 together in one detailed message because they interact, and handle 1 and 4 as separate, later steps.
options.B: Send only the most serious issue first, the NULL crash, and leave the other three until the migration runs without crashing at all.
options.C: Send all four in one message, so Claude has the complete list and can fix every problem in one pass before you re-run the migration script.
options.D: Send them one at a time in order 1, 2, 3, 4, re-running the migration after each, so every fix is isolated and easy to check.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.5: address multiple interacting issues in a single detailed message when fixes interact, versus sequential iteration for independent issues; provide specific test cases with example input and expected output to fix edge cases such as null values in migration scripts. For issue 1, give a specific test case: a row with a NULL email and the exact output you expect.

why_not.B: Postponing the interacting pair ignores that they need a joint fix.
why_not.C: Bundling independent issues with interacting ones blurs which change fixed what.
why_not.D: Fixing 2 and 3 separately means each fix can undo the other, since they interact.

questions.question:
Claude Code for CI/CD scenario. Your pipeline step is:

claude -p "Review the diff in pr.diff and list findings" --output-format json > out.json
jq '.result | fromjson | .findings[]' out.json | post_comments

The job runs and exits, but jq fails on about half the runs: .result sometimes holds prose with a findings list written as bullets. What is the right fix?

options.A: Wrap the jq step in a retry loop that re-runs the whole claude -p command until jq parses the output, with a limit of three runs.
options.B: Switch to --output-format stream-json and collect the streamed text chunks into one string before the jq step parses the findings list.
options.C: Add 'Return only valid JSON with a findings array and nothing else' to the prompt text, and keep reading the findings out of .result as before.
options.D: Add --json-schema with a schema for the findings (file, line, severity, message) and read them from the structured_output field of the JSON output.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.6: --output-format json and --json-schema enforce structured output in CI, producing machine-parseable findings for automated PR comments. With both flags, the validated output is in the structured_output field [code.claude.com/docs/en/headless]. --json-schema works in print mode only [code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference]. Current docs recommend `--bare` for scripted `-p` calls; it skips CLAUDE.md, hooks and MCP auto-discovery [code.claude.com/docs/en/headless].

why_not.A: Blind reruns cost time and money and still have no schema guarantee.
why_not.B: Streaming changes how output arrives, not whether it matches a schema.
why_not.C: A prompt line is not enforcement; the free-text result field can still hold prose.

questions.question: Claude Code for CI/CD scenario. Your review job runs on every push to a pull request. After the author pushes fixes, the job posts the same eight comments again, including three the author has already fixed. What should the re-run do?

options.A: Delete all of the bot's earlier comments before each run, so the pull request only ever shows the latest set of comments from the bot.
options.B: Include the earlier review's findings in the context and tell Claude to report only issues that are new or still not addressed in the latest commit.
options.C: Run the review only once per pull request, on the first push, so the author is not shown the same comment twice on later pushes.
options.D: Resume the session that wrote the code changes, so the reviewer already knows what was fixed and can skip those points automatically.

questions.rationale: Task statement 3.6: include prior review findings in context when re-running reviews after new commits, and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues to avoid duplicate comments.

why_not.A: Deleting history hides the duplicates instead of avoiding them and loses the record of what was raised.
why_not.C: Reviewing only once misses new problems introduced by later pushes.
why_not.D: The session that wrote the code is a weaker reviewer of its own changes (3.6 and 4.6 session isolation).

questions.question: Code generation scenario. The project CLAUDE.md says in bold: 'NEVER run terraform apply. Only run terraform plan.' The audit log shows Claude ran terraform apply twice this month while fixing infrastructure tests. Which change enforces this in configuration rather than relying on Claude to follow it?

options.A: Repeat the rule at the top and bottom of CLAUDE.md in capital letters, and add a short explanation of why applying from a laptop is dangerous.
options.B: Move the rule into a .claude/rules/terraform.md file with paths for **/*.tf, so it loads exactly when Claude touches Terraform files.
options.C: Add a deny rule such as "Bash(terraform apply *)" under permissions in the project's .claude/settings.json and commit it.
options.D: Create a /tf-plan skill that runs only terraform plan, and tell the team to always use the skill for infrastructure work.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.4: programmatic enforcement differs from prompt-based guidance; when compliance must be deterministic, prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate. Permission deny rules are enforced by Claude Code, and deny is evaluated before ask and allow [code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions]. A PreToolUse hook that exits 2 would also work. What changed since: the docs say a Bash deny rule 'isn't a security boundary' around the program [code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions]; for a hard guarantee, pair it with a PreToolUse hook or the sandbox.

why_not.A: CLAUDE.md is guidance; stronger wording lowers the rate but it is never zero (1.4).
why_not.B: A rule file is still guidance, just loaded at a better time.
why_not.D: A skill offers a safe path but doesn't stop Claude running apply directly.

options.A: The push runs: the allow rule is more specific than the deny rule, and the more specific rule takes precedence in Claude Code.
options.B: Claude Code asks the user to approve the push, because the allow and deny rules conflict and a conflict falls back to an ask prompt.
options.C: The push runs, because the allow list appears first in the file and Claude Code applies the first rule it reads in settings.json.
options.D: The push is blocked: deny rules are checked before allow rules, so the broad deny wins even though a narrower allow rule also matches.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.4 (enforcement through settings, not prompts). Exact rule: 'Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order determines the outcome, and rule specificity doesn't change the order.' An allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule [code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions].

why_not.A: Specificity doesn't change the order; an allow can't carve an exception out of a deny.
why_not.B: There is no conflict fallback; the first match in deny-ask-allow order decides.
why_not.C: Position in the file isn't the rule; the evaluation order is deny, then ask, then allow.

questions.question: Code generation scenario. Team policy: Claude may commit only after the unit tests have passed in this session. CLAUDE.md says so, and Claude follows it about 95% of the time. The other 5% have broken the main branch twice. You still want Claude to commit when tests pass. What should you add?

options.A: A deny rule for "Bash(git commit *)" in .claude/settings.json, so Claude is blocked from committing and a person does each commit by hand.
options.B: A second, louder line in CLAUDE.md that says 'Run the tests before you commit. This is mandatory.', placed right next to the existing rule.
options.C: A Stop hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes and reports the result, so the team can see which commits were made without tests.
options.D: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that, for git commit, checks for a fresh passing test run and exits 2 with a stderr message if none exists.

In Claude Code, PreToolUse exit code 2 blocks the tool call and stderr is shown to Claude [code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks].

why_not.A: A blanket deny blocks good commits too; the goal is a gate on a prerequisite, not a ban.
why_not.B: More prompt text still leaves a non-zero failure rate.
why_not.C: It reports after the fact; the bad commit has already happened.

questions.question:
Code generation scenario. A PreToolUse hook is registered with matcher "Edit|Write":

#!/bin/bash
f=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path')
if [[ "$f" == */migrations/* ]]; then
  echo "Migrations are locked. Ask a DBA." >&2
  exit 1
fi
exit 0

Claude still edits files in db/migrations/, and the transcript shows a 'hook error' notice each time. What is the smallest fix?

options.A: Add 'never edit files in migrations/' to CLAUDE.md as well, so Claude avoids the folder and the hook only has to catch the rare miss.
options.B: Register the same script as a PostToolUse hook, so it checks the file after the edit and reports the problem once the change is visible.
options.C: Change exit 1 to exit 2, so the hook always blocks the tool call and the stderr message is sent back to Claude.
options.D: Change the matcher to "*" so the hook runs for every tool, not only Edit and Write, and catches the migration edits whichever tool makes them.

questions.rationale: Task statements 1.4 and 1.5: hooks give deterministic enforcement only if they signal a block. Exact rule: for most hook events, exit code 2 is the only exit code that blocks through the code alone; 'Claude Code treats exit code 1 as a non-blocking error and proceeds with the action' [code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks].

why_not.A: Adding guidance doesn't repair the broken gate.
why_not.B: PostToolUse can't block; the edit has already happened.
why_not.D: The hook already runs for these edits; the exit code is what fails to block.

questions.question:
Code generation scenario. You want the unit tests for a module to run after every file change Claude makes, with failures sent back so Claude fixes them in the same task. In .claude/settings.json:

"hooks": {"PostToolUse": [{"matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "./scripts/run-unit-tests.sh"}]}]}

The script prints failures to stderr and exits 2 when a test fails. Claude edits src/tax.ts and breaks a test, but no failure ever reaches Claude. What is the smallest fix?

options.A: Change the matcher to "Edit|Write", so the hook runs after Claude's file edits and not only after Bash commands.
options.B: Make the script exit 1 instead of 2 on a failure, so the result shows as an error rather than a block in the transcript.
options.C: Change the event from PostToolUse to PreToolUse, so the tests run before each edit and stop a bad change early.
options.D: Add 'Run the unit tests after every edit and fix any failures' to CLAUDE.md, so Claude runs them itself as a backup.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.5 (PostToolUse hooks act on tool results, with hooks chosen over prompt guidance for guaranteed checks). The matcher decides which tools trigger the hook; Claude's file changes come through the Edit and Write tools, not Bash. For PostToolUse, exit 2 'Shows stderr to Claude; the tool already ran' [code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks].

why_not.B: Exit 1 is a non-blocking error, and the stderr is not fed to Claude the way it is on exit 2.
why_not.C: Before the edit, the new code isn't on disk yet, so the tests would check the old code.
why_not.D: This is guidance that can be skipped; the real fault is that the hook never fires on edits.

"hooks": {"PostToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write",

options.B: The edit is rolled back and src/cart.ts goes back to its earlier content, because exit 2 blocks the Edit tool call it came from.

options.D: The edit stays in place; the ESLint errors on stderr are shown to Claude, which can then fix the file in its next step.

You want every edit checked, with problems fed back so Claude fixes them in the same task. What should you set up?

options.B: A PreToolUse hook on Edit and Write that runs the linter, so problems are caught before each edit is applied to the file on disk.
options.C: A PostToolUse hook with matcher "Edit|Write" that runs the formatter and linter and exits 2 with the errors on stderr.
options.D: A nightly CI job that formats and lints the whole repository and opens a ticket for each file with problems, assigned to whoever last changed it.

why_not.A: Still guidance; it's the rule that already gets skipped.
why_not.B: PreToolUse is the point for blocking a call before it runs. Here the goal is to check the edited file and feed errors back so Claude fixes them, which PostToolUse does after each edit.
why_not.D: It catches problems a day late and outside the task, not in the same task.

questions.question:
Choose two. Code generation scenario. A PostToolUse hook on "Edit|Write" runs the type checker and ends like this:

  cat errs.txt >&2
fi
exit 0

Type errors are printed, but Claude never reacts to them. Which two changes would get the errors to Claude?

options.B: Change the hook to PreToolUse so the type check runs before each edit is applied to the file.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. The support agent's loop log shows this. Request 3 returns stop_reason "tool_use" with one tool_use block (id "toolu_01", name "lookup_invoice"). The code logs the block, then sends request 4 with the same messages plus a new user message whose only content is the text "Please continue." Request 4 fails with a 400 error. What is the smallest fix?

options.A: Raise max_tokens on request 4 and add a system prompt line telling Claude to finish its answer in text instead of calling tools, so the loop no longer depends on tool results to move forward.
options.B: Change the loop so it ends whenever the assistant message contains any text, so a tool_use turn with a short preamble counts as finished and request 4 is never sent at all.
options.C: Run lookup_invoice, then send request 4 with the assistant turn followed by a user message whose content starts with a tool_result block carrying tool_use_id "toolu_01" and the invoice data.
options.D: Retry request 4 with exponential backoff, because a 400 right after a tool_use turn usually means the API was briefly overloaded and the same payload will go through on a later attempt.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.1: when stop_reason is "tool_use", execute the requested tool and return its result for the next iteration. The API requires every tool_use block to be answered by a matching tool_result (same tool_use_id) in the next user message; leaving it out returns a 400 [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls].

why_not.A: This hides the bug by switching tool use off, which throws away model-driven tool choice instead of returning the result.
why_not.B: Checking for assistant text as a completion signal is an anti-pattern named in task statement 1.1, and the tool still never runs.
why_not.D: A 400 is a bad request, so resending the same payload fails again; backoff fits 429, 500 and 529, not 400.

questions.question: Request 6 in an agent loop sends this last user message: content = [ {"type": "text", "text": "Here is what the tool found:"}, {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_07", "content": "3 open tickets"} ]. The API returns a 400 error. What is wrong?

options.A: tool_result content has to be a JSON object rather than a plain string, so "3 open tickets" must be wrapped as {"result": "3 open tickets"} before the request will validate.
options.B: The tool_result block has to come before any text in that user message; put the tool_result first and the text after it, or drop the text line entirely.
options.C: The loop should have set is_error: true on the result, because a result sent with a text block next to it is treated by the API as a failed tool call.
options.D: Tool results belong in a new assistant message rather than a user message, because the assistant was the one that asked for the tool in the first place.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.1: tool results are appended to the conversation so the model can reason about the next step. The docs add the exact rule: in the user message that carries tool results, the tool_result blocks come first and any text comes after them; text first returns a 400 [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls].

why_not.A: A tool_result's content may be a plain string, so the string is not the problem.
why_not.C: is_error marks a tool that failed; it has nothing to do with block order and would mislead the model here.
why_not.D: tool_result blocks go in the user message that follows the assistant's tool_use, never in an assistant message.

questions.question: Multi-agent research scenario. A research agent sometimes stops after 2 tool calls with a half-done report, and sometimes runs 40 calls. The loop ends when the reply text contains "DONE" or when it reaches 10 iterations. Which change makes the stop decision correct while keeping a safety net?

options.A: Stop as soon as an assistant message contains any text block, since Claude only writes prose to the user once it has finished calling all of its tools.
options.B: Remove the text check and make 10 iterations the only stop rule, because a fixed cap is predictable, easy to test in staging and cannot be fooled by wording.
options.C: Loop while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stop when it is "end_turn"; keep a high iteration or cost limit only as a guard that hands the case to a person if it trips.
options.D: Keep the "DONE" check, but tell Claude in the system prompt to write DONE only after it has checked every source, and raise the cap from 10 to 25 so long tasks have room.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.1: continue when stop_reason is "tool_use" and terminate when it is "end_turn". The same task names three anti-patterns: parsing natural-language signals to end the loop, an arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stop, and treating assistant text as a completion sign. A cap is fine as a backstop, not as the signal.

why_not.A: Claude often writes text in the same turn as a tool call, so text is not a completion signal.
why_not.B: An arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stopping mechanism is the second anti-pattern, and it still cuts long tasks short.
why_not.D: It still ends the loop by parsing the reply text, which task statement 1.1 names as an anti-pattern.
