questions.question: Choose two. The loop log shows: turn 4 returns stop_reason "max_tokens" with a tool_use block whose input JSON is cut off mid-string; turn 9 returns stop_reason "end_turn". The current code runs every tool_use block it finds, whatever the stop_reason. Which two statements describe correct handling?

options.A: On turn 9, send one more request asking Claude to confirm it is finished, and stop only when its reply text says the task is complete.
options.B: Treat max_tokens the same as end_turn, because both mean Claude has stopped generating and the loop has nothing more it needs to do.
options.C: On turn 4, run the tool with whatever input could be parsed, and let the tool's own validation reject any missing field.
options.D: On turn 4, do not run the cut-off tool call; send the request again with a higher max_tokens so Claude can produce a complete tool call.
options.E: On turn 9, end the loop and return the final answer, because end_turn means Claude has finished its turn and asked for no more tools.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.1: stop_reason drives the loop, and "end_turn" ends it. "max_tokens" means the reply hit the token limit; the docs say a cut-off tool_use block should not be run and the request should be retried with a higher max_tokens [platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons].

why_not.A: Asking for a text confirmation is the natural-language completion check that task statement 1.1 calls an anti-pattern.
why_not.B: max_tokens means the reply was cut off, not finished, so treating it as end_turn drops unfinished work.
why_not.C: A truncated tool call is broken input; running it risks a wrong action instead of fixing the cut-off.

questions.question: Multi-agent research scenario. A coordinator runs three subagents: news, filings and analyst-notes. The trace shows the filings subagent sending its findings straight to the analyst-notes subagent, which then fails. The coordinator's final report says nothing about filings, and the coordinator log shows no error at all. What should the architect change first?

options.A: Give the subagents a shared scratch file they can all write to, so findings survive even when one subagent fails before the coordinator gets around to reading them.
options.B: Route every subagent result and error back through the coordinator, which decides what each next subagent receives and logs each failure it sees.
options.C: Add retries inside the analyst-notes subagent so it stops failing, and keep the direct hand-off between subagents because it saves a turn on every run.
options.D: Merge the three subagents into one large agent that holds all of their tools, so no hand-off between agents is needed and nothing can get lost between them.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.2: in hub-and-spoke orchestration the coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling and information routing. Routing all traffic through the coordinator gives observability, consistent error handling and controlled information flow, which is exactly what failed here.

why_not.A: A shared side channel still bypasses the coordinator, so failures stay invisible to it.
why_not.C: Retries treat this one failure but keep the peer-to-peer path that hid the error from the coordinator.
why_not.D: One agent with every tool degrades tool selection (task statement 2.3) and drops the coordinator's routing role.

questions.question: Multi-agent research scenario. A coordinator always runs its search, deep-analysis, fact-check and synthesis subagents, even for a question like "What year was this standard published?" Simple questions take minutes and cost as much as a deep report. The deep reports themselves are good. What is the best change?

options.A: Move every subagent to a smaller model so the full pipeline costs less on each question, whether it is a simple lookup or a deep report.
options.B: Add a second, cheaper pipeline with its own fixed sequence for simple questions, and pick between the two pipelines with a keyword list.
options.C: Keep the full pipeline but run all four subagents in parallel, so simple questions finish sooner even though every subagent still runs on every query.
options.D: Have the coordinator judge what each query needs and invoke only the subagents it requires, so simple lookups skip the deep steps.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.2: the coordinator decides which subagents to invoke based on query complexity, and the skill is designing coordinators that dynamically select subagents rather than always routing through the full pipeline.

why_not.A: It weakens the good deep reports and still runs four subagents for a one-line answer.
why_not.B: A keyword router is a brittle pre-set decision tree; the coordinator should judge each query itself.
why_not.C: Synthesis needs the other results first, and the cost of running every subagent stays the same.

questions.question: Multi-agent research scenario. A coordinator's Task call to the synthesis subagent has this prompt: "Write the final report using the findings above." The search and document-analysis results sit only in the coordinator's own conversation history. The synthesis output is generic and cites nothing. What is wrong, and what is the fix?

options.A: Add a line to the synthesis subagent's system prompt telling it to look back through the conversation for the findings before it starts writing the report.
options.B: The subagent should be started with fork_session from the coordinator's session, so it shares the coordinator's memory of the findings without copying them into the prompt.
options.C: The synthesis subagent needs a larger context window so it can see the coordinator's full history; move it to a model with more context and keep the prompt as it is.
options.D: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history; put the complete search and analysis findings, with their source metadata, directly into the Task prompt.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.3: subagent context must be explicitly provided in the prompt, because subagents do not automatically inherit parent context. The skill is including complete findings from prior agents directly in the subagent's prompt, using structured formats that keep source metadata attached.

why_not.A: The subagent has no access to the coordinator's conversation, so there is nothing for it to look back through.
why_not.B: fork_session branches a session to explore divergent approaches (task statement 1.7); it is not how a coordinator hands context to a Task subagent.
why_not.C: Context size is not the issue; the subagent never received the findings at all.

questions.question: Choose two. Multi-agent research scenario. A coordinator built with the Agent SDK never starts its three subagents. In an earlier test build it did start them, but one per turn, so a report took about three times longer than it needed to. Which two changes fix both problems?

options.A: Include "Task" in the coordinator's allowedTools, since the Task tool is the mechanism a coordinator uses to spawn subagents.
options.B: Have the coordinator emit all three Task tool calls in a single response, so the subagents run in parallel rather than across separate turns.
options.C: Chain the subagents so each one starts the next when it finishes, which removes the coordinator's turn between them and saves time.
options.D: Add a system prompt line telling the coordinator it is allowed to delegate, and repeat that line at the end of the prompt so it carries more weight.
options.E: Give each subagent the coordinator's full tool list, so any one of them can take over the work if the coordinator still does not delegate.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.3: the Task tool spawns subagents and allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke them (exam wording). Parallel subagents come from multiple Task calls in one coordinator response rather than across separate turns. What changed since: Claude now invokes subagents through the Agent tool; it appears as "Agent" in tool_use blocks but as "Task" in the system:init tools list, and the SDK examples put "Agent" in allowed_tools [code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents]. Also, `allowedTools` now only pre-approves tools; tools not listed stay available and fall through to the permission mode. To remove a tool use `disallowedTools`, and to make subagents available, define them in `agents` [code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions; code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents]. The exam answer is unchanged.

why_not.C: Chaining still runs the subagents one after another and takes routing away from the coordinator.
why_not.D: A prompt line cannot grant a tool the coordinator is not allowed to call.
why_not.E: Spreading every tool to every subagent breaks role scoping (task statement 2.3) and does not make the coordinator delegate.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. An airline-rebooking agent escalates to a human desk with this note: "Customer is upset about their flight. Please help." The desk staff cannot see the chat transcript, and each case takes about 6 minutes of re-asking questions. What should the escalation contain instead?

options.A: A sentiment score and the agent's own confidence that the case needs a person, so the desk can sort incoming escalations by urgency before reading them.
options.B: A link to the full chat transcript plus the raw tool outputs, so the person can read everything the agent saw and draw their own conclusions about the case.
options.C: A structured summary: customer and booking ID, the root cause found, what was already tried, the change or amount requested, and the recommended next action.
options.D: The same short note, plus an instruction that the person ask the customer to describe the problem again, so the details come straight from the customer.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.4: structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation include customer details, root cause analysis and recommended actions, compiled for human agents who lack access to the conversation transcript.

why_not.A: Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable proxies (task statement 5.2) and still carry none of the case facts.
why_not.B: The desk has no transcript access, and a raw dump makes the person dig instead of act.
why_not.D: Making the customer repeat everything is the failure the handoff package exists to prevent.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. Halfway through a three-part request (a damaged item, a missing refund and a change of address), the agent hits a policy gap on the refund and must escalate. The damage claim and the address change are already resolved. What should the escalation carry?

options.A: A request that the customer contact support again later, once the agent's policy prompt has been updated to cover this kind of refund.
options.B: The whole case reopened as one item, so the person re-checks the damage claim and the address change before touching the refund question at all.
options.C: Only the refund issue, because the person should not be distracted by parts of the case that are already closed and need no further action from anyone.
options.D: The customer ID, the refund's root cause and amount, the policy gap found, the recommended action, and a note that the other two items are resolved and how.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.4: a mid-process handoff carries customer details, root cause and recommended action, and multi-concern requests are split into distinct items. Saying which items are already resolved stops the person from redoing or contradicting finished work.

why_not.A: A policy gap is a reason to escalate now (task statement 5.2), not to push the customer away.
why_not.B: Reopening finished items wastes the reviewer's time and ignores the split into distinct items.
why_not.C: Leaving out the resolved items risks the person redoing them or giving the customer a conflicting answer.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. A bank-transfer agent has a code gate: send_transfer is blocked unless state.verified is true. The trace shows verify_account_holder returned {"status": "multiple_matches", "holders": ["H-201", "H-388"]}, and the code then set state.verified = True because the verification tool had been called. The transfer went through. What is wrong?

options.A: The check should move to a PostToolUse hook on send_transfer, so the transfer result is inspected after it runs and reversed if the holder was not verified.
options.B: multiple_matches should come back with is_error: true so the loop crashes, which guarantees the transfer cannot run later in that session.
options.C: The gate checks that the verification tool was called, not that it returned one verified holder ID; set the flag only on a single verified ID.
options.D: The gate should also be written into the system prompt, so the model knows not to call send_transfer after any multiple_matches result comes back.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.4: programmatic prerequisites block downstream tool calls until the prerequisite step has completed, for example until the lookup has returned a verified customer ID. Calling the tool is not the same as getting a verified result. A multiple-match result should lead to asking for more identifiers (task statement 5.2).

why_not.A: PostToolUse runs after the transfer has already happened, which is too late for a money movement.
why_not.B: Crashing the session is not a recovery path; the agent should ask for another identifier instead.
why_not.D: Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate; the bug is in the code gate, and a prompt line does not fix it.

questions.question: Choose two. Customer support scenario. A billing-dispute agent has a 25-turn limit. In one case it hits the limit while still waiting on a refund lookup. In another, the lookup tool throws an exception and the loop crashes. Both customers are left with no reply and no ticket. Which two safeguards fit?

options.A: Log both kinds of event to a dashboard, so the support team can review the stuck cases together at the end of each week.
options.B: Add a system prompt line telling the agent to wrap up politely when it senses it is about to run out of turns.
options.C: Make that escalation carry a handoff package: customer ID, the dispute, what was tried, and the recommended next step.
options.D: Raise the turn limit to 100 so the agent has more room to finish, and restart the loop automatically after any crash.
options.E: Wrap the loop in code so a hit limit or a crash always ends in an escalation to a person, never a silent stop.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.4: when compliance must be deterministic, prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate, so enforce it in code; and escalations to human agents who lack the transcript carry a structured handoff summary (customer ID, root cause, what was tried, recommended action). A session safeguard makes every session end in a resolution or an escalation, even when the loop hits its limit or a tool crashes. The limit stays a guard, not the stop signal (task statement 1.1). The 'every session ends in a resolution or an escalation' framing is the kit's Flow 4 (practice, not doc).

why_not.A: Weekly review finds stuck cases after the customer has already been abandoned; the safeguard has to act inside the session.
why_not.B: A prompt line cannot act after a crash, and the model has no reliable sense of how many turns it has left.
why_not.D: A bigger limit and blind restarts make the failure rarer or repeat it; neither guarantees the case ends in a resolution or an escalation.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. An Agent SDK PreToolUse hook on issue_credit reads tool_input.amount. Policy says credits over $250 need a manager. The trace for a $400 credit shows: the hook logs "over limit", returns an empty object, and the credit goes through. What is the smallest correct fix?

options.A: Add the $250 rule to the system prompt as well, so the model stops asking for large credits and the hook only needs to keep logging the ones that slip past.
options.B: Move the check to a PostToolUse hook, so it can read the confirmed credit amount from the tool result and then alert a manager about the large credit.
options.C: Have the hook return a deny permission decision with a reason for credits over $250, and route those cases to the manager-approval workflow instead.
options.D: Lower the threshold in the hook to $200, so there is a safety margin below the $250 policy line before anything gets logged as over the limit.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.5: hooks that intercept outgoing tool calls enforce compliance rules, blocking policy-violating actions and redirecting to an alternative workflow such as human escalation. A hook that only logs blocks nothing. In the Agent SDK a PreToolUse hook blocks by returning hookSpecificOutput with hookEventName (the event name from the hook input, here "PreToolUse"), permissionDecision "deny" and a permissionDecisionReason [code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks].

why_not.A: Prompt rules are probabilistic; the guarantee has to come from the hook actually blocking.
why_not.B: PostToolUse runs after the credit is issued, so it can only report the breach, not stop it.
why_not.D: Changing the number does not help when the hook never blocks anything.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. Three MCP tools return order dates as 1727222400, "2024-09-25T00:00:00Z" and "25/09/2024". The agent sometimes compares them wrongly and tells customers an order is late when it is not. Which fix guarantees one date format before Claude reasons over the data?

options.A: Add a convert_date tool and tell Claude to call it on every date it sees before comparing, so the conversion is done by code rather than by the model.
options.B: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts every date field in those three tools' results to ISO 8601 before the result reaches the model.
options.C: Add a system prompt rule that every date must be read as ISO 8601, with a few-shot example showing how to convert each of the three formats by hand.
options.D: Return all three formats side by side from each tool, so Claude can pick whichever one it trusts most for each comparison it needs to make.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.5: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them, for example normalizing Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 and other formats from different MCP tools. A hook is deterministic; prompts and optional tool calls are not.

why_not.A: Whether Claude calls the converter is still up to the model, so the guarantee is missing.
why_not.C: A prompt rule plus examples is probabilistic compliance, so some comparisons still go wrong.
why_not.D: More formats in context make the comparison harder, not reliable.

questions.question: A legal team runs the same four checks on every vendor contract: payment terms, liability caps, termination clauses and data-protection terms. The checks never change. One long prompt that does all four at once keeps missing problems in the termination clauses. Which decomposition fits best?

options.A: Prompt chaining: run a fixed sequence of focused steps, one per check, then a final step that combines the four results into one review.
options.B: Send the contract to four parallel agents that all get the same full four-check prompt, and take the majority answer for each check.
options.C: Keep the single prompt but move the termination check to the top, since the model reads the start of a long prompt most reliably.
options.D: Dynamic decomposition: let the agent decide after each clause which check to run next, based on what it has found in the contract so far.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.6: choose prompt chaining (fixed sequential steps) for predictable multi-aspect reviews, and dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation. The checks here are known in advance and never change, so a fixed chain of focused steps fits.

why_not.B: Four copies of the same overloaded prompt repeat the same blind spot four times.
why_not.C: Reordering one prompt keeps all four concerns competing for attention in the same pass.
why_not.D: Adaptive plans are for open-ended work; a fixed, known checklist does not need the agent to invent its steps.

questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 1.6 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Task: "Find out why checkout latency doubled last week." At step 1 the agent writes a plan: check the database, check the cache, check the CDN, write the report. At step 2 it finds that a new payment-provider SDK was deployed that same day, but it carries on with the cache and CDN checks, and the report blames the database. What should the decomposition do?

options.A: Split the four planned checks across four parallel subagents, so all of them finish faster and the report has more data to choose from.
options.B: Write a longer fixed plan at the start that also lists every SDK deployed recently, so the next run covers that lead in its proper order.
options.C: Use an adaptive plan: after each step, add or reorder subtasks based on what was found, so the new SDK becomes the next thing to investigate.
options.D: Add a final review step that asks the model to double-check the report for any cause it may have missed before sending it.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.6: open-ended investigation calls for dynamic, adaptive decomposition that generates subtasks based on what is discovered at each step. A plan frozen at step 1 cannot follow a lead found at step 2.

why_not.A: Running the same wrong plan faster does not add the SDK lead.
why_not.B: A longer fixed plan still cannot react to a lead nobody knew about at the start.
why_not.D: A self-check at the end does not change what was investigated, so the lead stays unexplored.

questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 1.6 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Choose two. Code generation scenario. You are asked to "add useful tests to a 10-year-old billing module that has none." Which two steps are the best way to break this open-ended task down?

options.A: First map the module's structure and find the high-impact areas, such as the code that computes invoices and taxes.
options.B: Build a prioritized test plan, and change it as you discover dependencies, such as a hidden currency-rounding helper.
options.C: Ask for a complete fixed test plan at the start and follow it exactly, so the work stays predictable from start to finish.
options.D: Generate one test for every public function in a single pass, then run them all at the end to see which ones fail.
options.E: Write tests file by file in alphabetical order, so coverage grows evenly across the module and no file is skipped.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.6: decompose open-ended tasks by first mapping structure, identifying high-impact areas, then creating a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.

why_not.C: A frozen plan cannot adapt when hidden dependencies turn up, which is the point of adaptive decomposition.
why_not.D: One blind pass skips the mapping and prioritizing steps.
why_not.E: Alphabetical order ignores impact, so the riskiest billing code may be tested last.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. Yesterday you ran a named Claude Code session, auth-audit, that read 30 files. Overnight a teammate changed two of them, session.py and tokens.py. Today you run claude --resume auth-audit and ask for the final findings. The answer quotes a function that no longer exists. What is the smallest fix?

options.A: Use --continue instead of --resume, because --continue reloads the files from disk while --resume only replays the saved tool results.
options.B: In the resumed session, tell Claude that session.py and tokens.py changed, and ask it to re-read and re-analyse just those two files.
options.C: Start a brand-new session and re-read all 30 files, because any change at all makes the whole earlier analysis untrustworthy.
options.D: Run /compact in the resumed session, so the old tool results are summarised and the stale details drop out of context.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.7: when resuming after code changes, inform the agent about the specific file changes for targeted re-analysis rather than requiring full re-exploration. Most of the earlier context (28 of 30 files) is still valid, so resuming fits. --continue just loads the most recent conversation in the current directory; it does not re-read files [code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference].

why_not.A: --continue picks the most recent session; neither flag re-reads files from disk.
why_not.C: Re-reading everything wastes the 28 files that did not change; targeted re-analysis is the stated skill.
why_not.D: Compacting summarises the stale results; it does not tell Claude which files changed.

questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 1.7 (Tier 1); code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. A two-week-old investigation session holds hundreds of tool results. Since then the service was refactored, and most of the files it read have moved or changed. You want to carry on from the conclusions it reached. Which approach is most reliable?

options.A: Resume with --resume and tell it that "some files changed", so it can work out which earlier tool results it can still trust.
options.B: Resume the session and run /compact first, so the old tool results are compressed into a summary before you continue the work.
options.C: Start a new session and inject a structured summary of the earlier conclusions, then let it read the current files fresh.
options.D: Fork the old session with fork_session, so the stale results stay in one branch while you do the new work in the other branch.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.7: starting a new session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results. Choose resumption when prior context is mostly valid, and a fresh start with injected summaries when the tool results are stale, as they are after a refactor.

why_not.A: A vague note leaves hundreds of stale results in context for Claude to trust by mistake.
why_not.B: A compacted summary of stale results is still built on stale results.
why_not.D: A fork copies the same stale baseline into the new branch.

questions.question: Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. After a shared codebase analysis, you want to compare two refactoring approaches side by side. Next week you also want to pick the original analysis up again by name. Which two choices fit?

options.A: Use fork_session from the shared analysis to create two independent branches, one for each refactoring approach.
options.B: Copy the analysis into CLAUDE.md, so every new session starts with it and no session ever needs to be resumed.
options.C: Resume the same session in two terminals and try one approach in each, since both terminals then share one history.
options.D: Run both approaches one after the other in the same session, then ask Claude to compare what it remembers of each one.
options.E: Give the investigation session a clear name, and continue it again next week with --resume <session-name>.

questions.rationale: Task statement 1.7: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches, and --resume <session-name> continues a named session (exam wording). In the current CLI the fork is --fork-session used with --resume; fork_session is the Python Agent SDK option [code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference].

why_not.B: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded standing rules, not a one-off analysis, and it loads in every session.
why_not.C: Two runs writing to one session are not independent branches, so the approaches mix.
why_not.D: In one session the second approach is shaped by the first, so the comparison is not clean.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. A customer writes: "This is the third time I've asked! My promo code didn't apply to order 5521." Applying a missed promo code is a standard action the agent is allowed to take. The customer has not asked for a person. What should the agent do?

options.A: Escalate to a person right away, because three contacts and angry wording show the case is too complex for the agent to handle well.
options.B: Apply the code silently and close the chat, since acknowledging the frustration only makes the reply longer and delays the fix.
options.C: Acknowledge the frustration, offer to apply the code now, and escalate only if the customer says again that they want a person.
options.D: Check the conversation's sentiment score; if it falls below the escalation threshold, hand off, and otherwise apply the code.

questions.rationale: Task statement 5.2: acknowledge frustration while offering resolution when the issue is within the agent's capability, and escalate only if the customer reiterates their preference. Sentiment-based escalation is an unreliable proxy for case complexity.

why_not.A: Anger is not complexity; this issue is simple and within the agent's power.
why_not.B: Ignoring the frustration skips the acknowledge-and-offer step the pattern asks for.
why_not.D: Sentiment-based escalation is named in task statement 5.2 as unreliable.

questions.objective: Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 5.2 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Choose two. Customer support scenario. You are writing the escalation rules for a returns agent. Which two situations should send the case to a person?

options.A: A customer asks to waive a restocking fee on a late-arriving gift, and the returns policy is silent on late gifts.
options.B: The customer types "I want to talk to a real person" before the agent has looked into the case at all.
options.C: The customer uses words like "furious" and "ridiculous" in an otherwise simple order-tracking question.
options.D: An account lookup returns two customers with the same name, so the agent hands the case off instead.
options.E: The agent's self-reported confidence in its own answer drops below 0.7 on a routine delivery question.

questions.rationale: Task statement 5.2: appropriate triggers are explicit requests for a human (honoured immediately, without investigating first), policy exceptions or gaps where policy is silent on the request, and inability to make progress. Multiple matches call for asking for more identifiers.

why_not.C: Sentiment-based escalation is also named as unreliable; the issue is simple.
why_not.D: Multiple matches call for asking for another identifier, not a handoff and not a guess.
why_not.E: Self-reported confidence is named as an unreliable proxy for case complexity.

questions.question: An agent has three search tools with overlapping descriptions: search_kb ("Searches content."), search_tickets ("Searches content for the user.") and search_forum ("Searches posts and content."). Logs show how-to questions go to search_tickets or search_forum about 40% of the time. What should you change first?

options.A: Rewrite each description to say what it searches (articles, past tickets, forum posts), its inputs and outputs, and when to use it over the other two.
options.B: Set temperature to 0 so the agent makes the same tool choice for the same question every time, and keep the three descriptions unchanged.
options.C: Set tool_choice to force search_kb on every turn, since how-to questions are by far the most common kind of request the agent receives.
options.D: Rename the tools to kb_lookup, ticket_lookup and forum_lookup so the names look less alike, and keep the three one-line descriptions as they are.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.1: tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection, and minimal or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting. The first fix is descriptions that clearly separate each tool's purpose, inputs, outputs and when to use it versus the similar tools.

why_not.B: Temperature 0 makes the choice repeatable, not right; the same wrong tool gets picked every time.
why_not.C: Forcing one tool breaks every ticket and forum question.
why_not.D: New names on top of empty descriptions still leave the model almost nothing to choose by.

questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. A generic process_document tool is used to pull numbers out of reports, write summaries and check claims against a source. Its outputs vary in shape from call to call, and downstream code often fails to parse them. What is the best redesign?

options.A: Keep process_document but add a mode string parameter, and describe all three modes and their output shapes in one long description.
options.B: Keep the tool as it is, and add a JSON example of each output shape to the system prompt so the model copies the right one each time.
options.C: Split it into purpose-specific tools (extract_figures, summarize_document, check_claim_against_source), each with its own contract.
options.D: Wrap the tool's output in a retry loop that asks the model to reformat its answer whenever the downstream parser fails on it.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.1: split generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts, so each tool's purpose and output shape is clear.

why_not.A: One tool with modes keeps the vague boundary and puts it inside a parameter.
why_not.B: Prompt examples ask for a shape but give no contract, so outputs still drift.
why_not.D: Retrying treats the symptom and adds cost; the interface itself stays unclear.

questions.objective: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1).

questions.question: fetch_policy_doc and query_claims_db both have clear, distinct, detailed descriptions. The system prompt says: "Whenever the user mentions a claim, always look it up right away." The agent now calls query_claims_db for questions like "What does my policy claim to cover?" What is the best fix?

options.A: Rewrite the keyword-triggered instruction in the system prompt so the word "claim" no longer ties every mention to a database lookup.
options.B: Remove fetch_policy_doc and answer coverage questions from policy text pasted into the system prompt instead of from a tool.
options.C: Rename query_claims_db to query_db, so the word claim no longer appears in the tool's name and cannot pull the model toward it.
options.D: Make fetch_policy_doc's description longer and more detailed, so it outweighs the system prompt line when the two point in different directions.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.1: system prompt wording affects tool selection, and keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations that override well-written tool descriptions. The skill is reviewing the system prompt for such instructions.

why_not.B: Removing a working tool trades one problem for a stale, bloated prompt.
why_not.C: A vaguer name hurts selection and leaves the keyword instruction in the prompt.
why_not.D: The descriptions are already good; the cause is the prompt line, which stays in place.

questions.question: Customer support scenario. An MCP tool, update_shipment, returns this body for every kind of failure: {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "failed"}], "isError": true}. The agent retries an invalid tracking number 5 times, and tells a user whose permission has expired to "try again later". What is the best fix?

options.A: Remove isError, so the agent reads "failed" as ordinary text and decides for itself what went wrong and what to do next.
options.B: Return structured error metadata: an error category, whether it is retryable, and a plain description of the problem.
options.C: Keep the body as it is but cap retries at 2 in the agent loop, so wasted calls drop and the user gets an answer sooner.
options.D: Add a system prompt line telling the agent not to retry update_shipment more than once, whatever the error text says.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.2: uniform errors like "Operation failed" stop the agent from choosing the right recovery; return structured metadata such as errorCategory (transient, validation, permission; business errors are a fourth kind in 2.2), isRetryable and a human-readable description (exam wording; these field names are a practice pattern, not MCP spec fields). The MCP spec's isError flag marks a tool failure the agent can see and react to [modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools].

why_not.A: Without isError the failure looks like a successful result, which is worse.
why_not.C: A cap still wastes retries on input that can never succeed and still mislabels the permission case.
why_not.D: A blanket retry rule also blocks retries on real transient errors, where a retry would help.

questions.objective: Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1); modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools.

questions.question: Choose two. Customer support scenario. A returns tool rejects a request because the purchase is past the 60-day return window. Which two things should its error response include so the agent handles the case well?

options.A: A short customer-friendly explanation of the 60-day rule that the agent can pass on.
options.B: Only the HTTP status 403, since the agent can tell from the code alone what went wrong.
options.C: A business-error category with retryable set to false, so the agent knows a retry cannot succeed.
options.D: isRetryable set to true, in case the date check was a brief timing glitch on the server.
options.E: A generic "Operation failed" message, so no internal policy detail reaches the model or customer.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.2: for business rule violations, include retriable: false flags and customer-friendly explanations so the agent can communicate appropriately; business errors are a distinct category from transient, validation and permission errors.

why_not.B: 403 suggests a permission problem, which is the wrong category, and a bare code gives the agent nothing to tell the customer.
why_not.D: A policy rejection will fail the same way every time, so retrying wastes calls.
why_not.E: A generic message is the anti-pattern that blocks good recovery decisions.

questions.objective: Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Customer support scenario. search_warranties returns {"isError": false, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "[]"}]} both when a serial number truly has no warranty and when the warranty database times out. What is the problem, and what is the fix?

options.A: The timeout is reported as an empty success; return it as a transient, retryable error, and keep [] for real no-match queries.
options.B: The tool should keep retrying the database inside the server until it answers, so the agent only ever gets real results.
options.C: An empty list should be sent with isError: true, because getting no data back is a failure from the agent's point of view.
options.D: The agent should treat every [] as a possible timeout, and call the tool a second time before it gives the user an answer.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.2: distinguish access failures, which need retry decisions, from valid empty results, which are successful queries with no matches. Mixing them makes the agent tell users there is no warranty when the lookup never ran.

why_not.B: Endless retries hang the call; local recovery should be bounded and then report the failure.
why_not.C: A real no-match is a successful query; flagging it as an error triggers useless retries.
why_not.D: Doubling every empty call wastes requests and still cannot tell the two cases apart.

questions.question: Multi-agent research scenario. A report-writing subagent's config lists 17 tools, including web_search, run_sql, send_email and deploy_preview. Its only job is to turn the findings it is given into a report. Traces show it runs web searches in the middle of reports and picks the wrong tool about 1 time in 6. What is the best fix?

options.A: Move the report writer to a larger, more capable model, which copes better with long tool lists and many similar-looking choices.
options.B: Write longer, more detailed descriptions for all 17 tools, so the report writer can tell them apart more easily when it chooses.
options.C: Cut its tools to the few its role needs, such as reading findings and formatting sections, and route new research via the coordinator.
options.D: Add a system prompt rule listing which of the 17 tools the report writer must never call, and keep the full list for unusual reports.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3: too many tools (for example 18 instead of 4 to 5) degrade tool selection, and agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them. Restrict each subagent to the tools its role needs and route complex cases through the coordinator.

why_not.A: Wrong picks come from 17 tools, many outside the role; a bigger model still has those out-of-role tools in reach.
why_not.B: Better descriptions help selection but leave 17 choices and out-of-role tools in reach.
why_not.D: A deny list in the prompt is probabilistic and leaves the large tool set in place.

questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Structured data extraction scenario. A document-intake agent has a generic fetch_url tool. It sometimes fetches tracking pages and login screens instead of the policy PDFs it is meant to load, and those pages end up in its analysis. What is the best change?

options.A: Add a line to fetch_url's description saying "only use for documents", and keep the generic tool for flexibility.
options.B: Keep fetch_url and add a line to the agent's prompt telling it to ignore any fetched page that turns out not to be a policy PDF.
options.C: Remove the tool entirely and ask users to paste the text of each policy document into the chat by hand instead.
options.D: Replace fetch_url with a load_document tool that checks the URL points to an allowed document before it fetches anything.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3: replace generic tools with constrained alternatives, for example replacing fetch_url with a load_document tool that validates document URLs. The constraint lives in the tool, so the misuse cannot happen.

why_not.A: A description line asks for good behaviour but the generic tool can still fetch anything.
why_not.B: The wrong page is already fetched and in context; the prompt only hopes it is ignored.
why_not.C: Removing the tool breaks the workflow instead of constraining it.

questions.question: Choose two. A contract-drafting agent often needs to look up a clause number in the master agreement. Each lookup takes a full round trip through the coordinator and a legal-research agent. Now and then the drafter also needs real legal research. Which two changes fit?

options.A: Merge the drafting and research agents into one agent, so lookups and research happen in a single context.
options.B: Give the drafting agent all of the research agent's tools, so it no longer has to wait for the coordinator.
options.C: Paste the whole master agreement into the drafter's system prompt and take the coordinator out of the flow.
options.D: Keep sending the rarer real legal research requests through the coordinator to the research agent.
options.E: Give the drafting agent one narrow lookup_clause tool for the frequent clause-number check it keeps needing.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.3: provide scoped cross-role tools for high-frequency needs while routing complex cases through the coordinator, and keep each agent's tool set limited to its role.

why_not.A: Merging roles grows the tool set and loses the coordinator's routing.
why_not.B: Handing over every research tool causes cross-specialization misuse and a bigger tool list.
why_not.C: Removing the coordinator also removes the route for the complex research cases.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. A teammate clones the repo. Its committed .mcp.json contains: {"mcpServers": {"tracker": {"type": "http", "url": "https://tracker.example.com/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}"}}}}. TRACKER_TOKEN is not set on the teammate's machine, and the tracker server rejects their requests. What is the right fix?

options.A: Remove the headers block from .mcp.json, so the tracker falls back to read-only access for people without a token.
options.B: Have the teammate set TRACKER_TOKEN in their own environment, and keep ${TRACKER_TOKEN} in the committed .mcp.json.
options.C: Copy the original author's ~/.claude.json into the repo, so the teammate picks up the token the author has stored.
options.D: Paste the teammate's own token into the Authorization header in .mcp.json and commit it, so every new clone works.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.4: .mcp.json uses environment variable expansion such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} so credentials are never committed; each person supplies the value in their own environment. Docs detail (not in the exam guide): when a variable is unset and has no default, Claude Code warns in claude mcp list and /mcp and loads the server with the ${VAR} text unexpanded, except that in a remote server's url and headers (as here) some credential variables read as empty instead, with no warning; a ${VAR:-default} fallback is also supported [code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp, checked 2026-10-07].

why_not.A: Dropping the header doesn't grant access; the server still needs a credential, supplied per person through the variable.
why_not.C: ~/.claude.json is one person's user config; putting it in git leaks the author's credentials.
why_not.D: Committing a token is exactly what ${VAR} expansion in .mcp.json exists to prevent.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. Your team wants everyone working in one repo to use the same GitHub MCP server, without anyone committing a personal access token. Where and how should the server be configured?

options.A: In CLAUDE.md, with instructions telling Claude which server URL to call and which token to send with each of its requests.
options.B: In the project's .mcp.json, committed to git, with the token written as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} so each person's environment supplies it.
options.C: In .mcp.json with the token pasted in, and the file added to .gitignore so the token stays private to whoever created the file.
options.D: In each developer's ~/.claude.json with their own token pasted in, plus a README section telling new joiners to copy the block into theirs.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.4: configure shared MCP servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion for authentication tokens. The file is shared through version control; the secret stays in each person's environment. Project-scoped servers ask each user for approval before first use [code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp].

why_not.A: CLAUDE.md gives instructions; it does not configure MCP servers, and it would expose the token.
why_not.C: A gitignored file is not shared, which defeats the point of a team server.
why_not.D: User-level config is personal, so the shared setup drifts and depends on copy-paste.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. You want .mcp.json to use the INTERNAL_API_URL environment variable when it is set, and to fall back to https://api.internal.example.com when it is not. Which url value does Claude Code expand that way?

options.A: "url": "${INTERNAL_API_URL:-https://api.internal.example.com}", using the variable-with-default form.
options.B: "url": "%INTERNAL_API_URL%", with the fallback value placed in a separate "defaults" key next to mcpServers.
options.C: "url": "{{INTERNAL_API_URL | default: 'https://api.internal.example.com'}}", using a template filter.
options.D: "url": "$INTERNAL_API_URL || https://api.internal.example.com", using a shell-style fallback.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.4: environment variable expansion in .mcp.json. Claude Code supports ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} in command, args, env, url and headers [code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp]. The other forms are not supported syntax.

why_not.B: %VAR% is Windows shell syntax, and .mcp.json has no defaults key.
why_not.C: Template filters are not part of .mcp.json expansion.
why_not.D: $VAR || value is shell logic, not the expansion syntax Claude Code reads in .mcp.json.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. You want to try an experimental MCP server for a week, in all of your projects, without any of your teammates seeing it or getting a prompt about it. Where should it be configured?

options.A: In your user-level configuration (~/.claude.json), for example by adding it with claude mcp add --scope user.
options.B: In the project's .claude/settings.json under an mcpServers key, where Claude Code keeps its tool setup.
options.C: In each repo's .mcp.json, on a local branch that you keep unpushed, so teammates don't pull the change in.
options.D: In CLAUDE.md at the repo root, with a note that marks the server as personal so teammates' sessions all skip it.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.4: personal or experimental MCP servers go in user-scoped ~/.claude.json, which is not shared through version control. The docs' user scope makes a server available across all your projects [code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp].

why_not.B: Claude Code reads MCP server definitions from .mcp.json or ~/.claude.json, not from .claude/settings.json, and that settings file is shared with the team anyway.
why_not.C: A per-repo file on unpushed branches must be repeated in every repo and is easy to push by mistake.
why_not.D: CLAUDE.md holds instructions, not server configuration, and it is committed for everyone.

questions.question: Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. In one repo, Priya adds a database MCP server with claude mcp add and no --scope flag. Sam adds a shared ticket server to the project's .mcp.json and commits it. Teammates then pull and open the repo in interactive Claude Code sessions. Which two statements are true?

options.A: Sam's server is project scope: every teammate who pulls gets it, and Claude Code asks each of them to approve it first.
options.B: Both servers are user scope, so each one is available to its owner in every project on that person's machine.
options.C: Priya's server is shared with the team, because a server added inside a repo is saved to that repo's .mcp.json by default.
options.D: Sam's server loads silently for every teammate the moment they pull, with no prompt, because it is committed to git.
options.E: Priya's server is local scope: private to her, available only in this project, and stored in her own ~/.claude.json.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.4: project-level .mcp.json is for shared team tooling, and user-level ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers (exam wording). Current docs add a third level: local scope is the default for claude mcp add, private to you in the current project and stored in ~/.claude.json; project scope lives in .mcp.json and, in an interactive session, asks each user for approval before first use (in claude -p, Agent SDK and cloud sessions it loads without asking); user scope (--scope user) covers all your projects [code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp]. What changed since: the exam guide names only project and user levels; local is the docs' default.

why_not.B: User scope needs --scope user; Priya's server is local and Sam's is project.
why_not.C: The default scope is local, not project, so nothing is written to .mcp.json.
why_not.D: In an interactive session, Claude Code asks for approval before it uses project-scoped servers from .mcp.json.

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. In a large monorepo, Claude runs Grep for the pattern "Logger" across the whole repo with full matching-line output. The result is thousands of lines, and the session's context fills up before it finds the one call site you asked about. What should the search have done?

options.A: Grep a narrower pattern, list the matching files first, then show content only in the few files that matter.
options.B: Run /compact before running the search, so there is enough free room in context for all of the matching lines.
options.C: Use Glob with the pattern "Logger" instead, since Glob is the faster search tool and returns shorter results than Grep.
options.D: Read every file under src/ first so Claude has the full context of the code, then answer the question from what it has read.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.5: build codebase understanding incrementally, starting with Grep to find entry points and then Read to follow the flow, rather than loading everything up front. A narrow pattern and a files-only first pass keep the output small. (Claude Code's Grep tool has a files-only output mode; the parameter name is from the tool schema, not a doc page, so treat it as unconfirmed.)

why_not.B: Compacting first does not shrink a search that returns thousands of lines.
why_not.C: Glob matches file paths, not file contents, so it cannot find call sites.
why_not.D: Reading all files up front is the exact anti-pattern the task statement warns about.

questions.objective: Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.5 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Developer productivity scenario. Claude calls Edit on config.py to change "timeout = 30" to "timeout = 60". The edit fails because "timeout = 30" appears in three places in the file. You want only the one in the retry section changed. What is the most reliable next step?

options.A: Use a longer anchor unique to the retry section; if none exists, Read the whole file and Write back the corrected version.
options.B: Use Grep to count how many matches there are, then ask the user to change the right line in the file by hand.
options.C: Retry the same Edit call unchanged, since edits on large files sometimes fail on the first attempt and then succeed.
options.D: Use Bash with sed to replace every "timeout = 30" in the file at once, then check the diff afterwards for problems.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.5: Edit makes targeted changes using unique text matching. When Edit cannot find unique anchor text, use Read to load the full file followed by Write as a reliable fallback.

why_not.B: Handing the edit back to the user skips a reliable tool path that exists.
why_not.C: The text is still not unique, so the same call fails the same way.
why_not.D: Replacing all three changes two lines you wanted to keep.

questions.objective: Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively
questions.source: Project-authored. CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, task statement 2.5 (Tier 1).

questions.question: Choose two. Developer productivity scenario. You need to (1) find every test file named like *.spec.ts anywhere in the repo, and (2) find every place that calls a helper which a wrapper module re-exports under two different names. Which two moves are right?

options.A: Grep only for the helper's original name, since re-exported functions keep the same name everywhere.
options.B: Find all the names the wrapper exports for the helper, then Grep for each of those names across the codebase.
options.C: Use Glob with the pattern **/*.spec.ts to find every test file by its name, wherever it sits in the repo.
options.D: Read the wrapper module and every file that imports it, all at the start, before searching for anything.
options.E: Use Grep with the pattern "spec.ts" to find the test files by searching for that text inside their contents.

questions.rationale: Task statement 2.5: Glob finds files by naming pattern (for example **/*.test.tsx), Grep searches file contents, and tracing usage across wrapper modules means first identifying all exported names, then searching for each name.

why_not.A: The wrapper exports the helper under other names, so a search for one name misses callers.
why_not.D: Reading everything up front wastes context; build understanding incrementally.
why_not.E: Grep searches contents, so it finds files that mention spec.ts rather than files named that way.
